Adversarial Search

Minimax, Alpha-Beta Pruning, Expectiminimax

Search when somebody else chooses every second move — and they want you to lose.

Until now the world was neutral. Roads do not move while you drive on them. In a game, an opponent picks every second move, and picks the move that is worst for you. That single change turns search into a new problem — and gives us the algorithms that beat the world chess champion in 1997.

Learning objectives

  • Describe a two-player zero-sum game as a search problem.
  • Trace the minimax algorithm on a game tree and read off the best move.
  • Apply alpha-beta pruning by hand and explain why move ordering matters so much.
  • Use an evaluation function and a cutoff test to play under a time limit.
  • Extend minimax to games with dice using expectiminimax.

Key terms in this module

Adversarial search say: ad-ver-SAIR-ee-al
Search where another agent chooses some of the moves and wants the opposite result to you.
Zero-sum game
Whatever one player gains, the other loses by the same amount. Chess and tic-tac-toe are zero-sum.
Game tree
The tree of all possible move sequences. Levels alternate between the two players.
MAX
The player we are deciding for. MAX wants the largest final value.
MIN
The opponent. MIN wants the smallest final value.
Ply say: rhymes with 'fly'
One move by one player. Two plies (one move each) make a full round.
Terminal state
A finished position: win, lose, or draw. Its value comes from the rules.
Utility / payoff
The number given to a terminal state, e.g. +1 win, 0 draw, −1 loss. It is Module 2's utility function, applied to finished games.
Minimax value
The value of a position assuming both players play their best from there on.
Alpha-beta pruning say: AL-fa BAY-ta
Skipping branches that cannot change the final decision. Same answer as minimax, far less work.
Alpha (α)
The best value MAX can already guarantee on the path so far.
Beta (β)
The best value MIN can already guarantee on the path so far.
Evaluation function
A quick guess at how good a non-final position is, used when we cannot search to the end.
Cutoff test
The rule that stops the search early — usually a depth limit or a time limit.
Horizon effect
A problem where the search stops just before a bad event, so it never sees it coming.
Expectiminimax
Minimax plus chance nodes, for games with dice or shuffled cards. Chance nodes take the average, weighted by probability.
Section 5.1

A game is a search problem with an enemy

You can describe a game with the same five parts from Module 3 — with two changes that make everything harder.

In the terms of section 2.4, a game is a competitive multi-agent task environment: another agent acts, and it wants the opposite of what you want.

Module 3 search

You control every step

  • You pick the whole path
  • The world does not fight back
  • Answer = a sequence of actions
  • Cost is added along the way
Adversarial search

You control every second step

  • The opponent picks the alternate moves
  • They choose what is worst for you
  • Answer = a strategy: a reply to every reply
  • Value comes at the end, from the result

We study two-player zero-sum games with perfect information: two players take turns, both can see the whole position, and one player's gain is exactly the other's loss. Tic-tac-toe, chess, and checkers all fit.

The vocabulary

The two players are called MAX and MIN. MAX is the player we are deciding for and wants the highest value; MIN is the opponent and wants the lowest. Finished positions get a utility: +1 for a MAX win, 0 for a draw, −1 for a loss. One move by one player is a ply.

Planning around someone who will not help you

You are arranging a match schedule with someone who gets to pick every second slot, and who will always pick the slot that is worst for you. You cannot plan a single line and hope. You must plan a reply for every reply: "if he takes Tuesday, I take Thursday; if he takes Thursday, I take Tuesday."

That is why the answer to a game is not a path — it is a strategy.

Why games became AI's laboratory

Games have simple rules and an unarguable score, so an algorithm can be tested honestly. They are also far too large to solve by brute force: chess has roughly 35 legal moves per position and games run about 50 moves each side, which gives a tree with more nodes than there are atoms in anything you can imagine. Every technique in this module exists because that tree cannot be searched.

5 min read

Section 5.2

Minimax: assume the opponent plays perfectly

The core idea is one sentence: at MAX levels take the largest child value, at MIN levels take the smallest, and pass the result upward.

Notice that MAX does not get 12. MIN would never allow it.
def minimax(state, game):
    """Return the best move for the player about to move."""
    player = game.to_move(state)

    def max_value(state):
        if game.is_terminal(state):
            return game.utility(state, player)
        return max(min_value(game.result(state, a)) for a in game.actions(state))

    def min_value(state):
        if game.is_terminal(state):
            return game.utility(state, player)
        return min(max_value(game.result(state, a)) for a in game.actions(state))

    return max(game.actions(state),
               key=lambda a: min_value(game.result(state, a)))
i
Minimax is pessimistic on purpose

It assumes the opponent always finds their best reply. If the opponent plays badly, you do at least as well as minimax promised — never worse. That is why the assumption is safe even when it is wrong.

Cost: minimax is depth-first search over the game tree, so time is $O(b^m)$ and memory is $O(bm)$, where $b$ is the number of legal moves and $m$ is the depth. For tic-tac-toe that is fine. For chess it is impossible — which is the next two sections.

Check yourself

In the tree above, a student says "MAX should play right, because 8 is the biggest number there." What is wrong?

Show answer

MAX does not choose the leaf — MIN does, one level down. If MAX goes right, MIN will choose 2, not 8. The value of the right branch is therefore 2, and the left branch, worth 3, is better. Always evaluate a branch by what the opponent will allow, not by its best leaf.

7 min read

Section 5.3

Alpha-beta pruning: skipping what cannot matter

Minimax examines every leaf. Most of them cannot possibly change the decision. Alpha-beta finds those and skips them — and it returns exactly the same move as minimax. This is not an approximation.

Buying a car

You have already found a good car for 60,000 riyals. At the next showroom the salesman says the cheapest car he has starts at 75,000. You do not need to see the rest of his cars, ask about colours, or take a test drive. Nothing he can show you will beat the offer you already have.

That is pruning: one fact made a whole branch irrelevant.

α (alpha) is the best value MAX can already guarantee along the current path. β (beta) is the best value MIN can already guarantee. When α ≥ β, stop examining this node's remaining children — nobody will ever choose to come here.

Walk through it once

Take the same tree. MAX explores the left branch first and learns its value is 3, so α = 3: MAX is guaranteed at least 3.

Now MAX starts the right branch, a MIN node. The first child is 2, so this MIN node will return at most 2 — MIN can already guarantee 2 or better for itself. Compare: α = 3 and β = 2, so α ≥ β. Whatever the other child holds, MIN will never return more than 2, and MAX already has 3. Skip the remaining child completely. In this tiny tree we saved one leaf. In a real game tree that same logic removes millions.

def alpha_beta(state, game):
    def max_value(state, alpha, beta):
        if game.is_terminal(state):
            return game.utility(state)
        v = -float('inf')
        for a in game.actions(state):
            v = max(v, min_value(game.result(state, a), alpha, beta))
            if v >= beta:
                return v            # MIN would avoid this node — prune
            alpha = max(alpha, v)
        return v

    def min_value(state, alpha, beta):
        if game.is_terminal(state):
            return game.utility(state)
        v = float('inf')
        for a in game.actions(state):
            v = min(v, max_value(game.result(state, a), alpha, beta))
            if v <= alpha:
                return v            # MAX would avoid this node — prune
            beta = min(beta, v)
        return v

    return max(game.actions(state),
               key=lambda a: min_value(game.result(state, a),
                                       -float('inf'), float('inf')))

Move ordering decides how much you save

Worst order

Best moves examined last

  • Almost nothing can be pruned
  • Time stays O(b^m)
  • Same cost as plain minimax
Perfect order

Best moves examined first

  • Time falls to about O(b^(m/2))
  • Same time now searches twice as deep
  • Effective branching factor drops from b to about √b
Twice as deep is the whole game

In chess, searching two extra plies is roughly the difference between a club player and a strong one. That is why engines spend real effort guessing a good move order before searching: try captures first, try the move that was best at the previous shallower depth, keep a table of positions already seen. The ordering is not a detail — it is where the strength comes from.

8 min read

Section 5.4

Playing under a clock: evaluation and cutoff

Even with alpha-beta, chess cannot be searched to the end. So we stop early and guess the value of the position we stopped at.

This is the semi-dynamic environment of section 2.4: the board waits while you think, but the clock does not.

  1. Replace the terminal test with a cutoff test

    Stop at a fixed depth, or when the clock says stop.

  2. Replace utility with an evaluation function

    A quick formula that estimates how good this position is for MAX.

An evaluation function gives a number for a non-final position. In chess the classic form is a weighted sum of features: material (pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9), control of the centre, king safety, pawn structure. It must be fast, because it runs on millions of positions.

!
The horizon effect

Search 6 plies deep and the program is blind to anything that happens on ply 7. A program can even learn to delay disaster with pointless moves that push the bad event just past its horizon — and then feel satisfied. The standard cure is to search unstable positions a little deeper (captures and checks) before trusting the evaluation, so you never stop in the middle of an exchange.

Iterative deepening, again

Module 3's trick returns here for a different reason. Search to depth 2 and keep the best move. Then depth 3, then 4, until the clock runs out — and play the best move from the deepest search that finished. You always have an answer ready, and the results of shallow searches give you the move ordering that makes alpha-beta so much faster at the next depth.

♟️ Deep Blue, 1997

Beat world champion Garry Kasparov using alpha-beta with a hand-built evaluation function and special hardware. Classical search, not learning.

🎮 Game opponents

The difficulty setting in many games is simply the search depth the computer is allowed.

🤝 Negotiation and auctions

Any setting where another party responds to your move with their own interest in mind.

🛡️ Security planning

Placing checks and patrols against someone who will adapt to whatever you do.

6 min read

Section 5.5

When luck joins the game: expectiminimax

Backgammon has dice. Card games have a shuffle. The opponent is still against you, but now a third thing decides part of the outcome: chance. This is the stochastic case from section 2.4: the same move can lead to different results.

Expectiminimax adds a third kind of node. MAX nodes take the maximum, MIN nodes take the minimum, and chance nodes take the average of their children, weighted by probability.

Not the best case, not the worst case — the expected case.
!
Now the exact numbers matter

In plain minimax, only the order of the values matters: any evaluation function that ranks positions the same way produces the same move. With chance nodes that is no longer true. Doubling one value changes an average, and so can change the decision. Your evaluation numbers must be meaningful on a real scale, not just correctly ordered.

The cost: the branching factor now includes every dice roll, so the tree explodes and useful depth drops sharply. Pruning is still possible but much weaker, because a chance node's average cannot be bounded until you have looked at most of its children.

Check yourself

Why can alpha-beta prune so much less in a game with dice?

Show answer

Pruning works because a MIN node can only go down as you see more children, and a MAX node can only go up, so a bound is known early. A chance node computes an average, which can move up or down with every new child. Without a firm bound you cannot safely skip the rest — unless you know the range the values must lie in, which allows a weaker form of pruning.

Revision card

Module 5 cheat sheet

Setup

  • Two players, zero-sum, perfect information
  • MAX wants the largest value, MIN the smallest
  • Ply = one move by one player
  • The answer is a strategy, not a single path

Minimax

  • MAX level → take the maximum child
  • MIN level → take the minimum child
  • Assumes the opponent plays perfectly (safe assumption)
  • Time O(b^m), memory O(bm)

Alpha-beta

  • α = best MAX can guarantee so far
  • β = best MIN can guarantee so far
  • Prune when α ≥ β
  • Returns exactly the same move as minimax
  • Perfect ordering → O(b^(m/2)) = twice the depth in the same time

Playing in real time

  • Replace terminal test with a cutoff test (depth or clock)
  • Replace utility with an evaluation function (fast, weighted features)
  • Iterative deepening keeps an answer ready and improves move ordering
  • Horizon effect: trouble just past the search depth is invisible

Expectiminimax

  • Adds chance nodes for dice and shuffles
  • Chance node value = Σ probability × child value
  • Exact evaluation numbers now matter, not just their order
  • Much less pruning is possible

Mistakes that cost marks

  • Reading a branch's value from its best leaf instead of what the opponent allows
  • Saying alpha-beta gives an approximate answer — it gives the exact minimax move
  • Pruning when α > β only — the condition is α ≥ β
  • Forgetting that move ordering is what makes alpha-beta fast
  • Using plain minimax for a game with dice
